--- title: "The 2PL Is a Tiny Neural Network: Width, Depth, and Held-Out Prediction" description: | The Rasch and 2PL models are two-embedding networks with no hidden layer. Part I builds them in PyTorch and checks them against `mirt`. Part II widens and deepens them and asks, on 24 IRW tables scored with the InterModel Vigorish, whether a neural network predicts held-out item responses any better than the 2PL. On most of these tables it does not; where one does, an ordinary two-dimensional MIRT usually does about as well as the multilayer perceptrons. Part III takes apart a small gap between the torch 2PL and the `mirt` 2PL: fitting by marginal likelihood and predicting from the posterior closes it, and fixing the scale of the person parameters does not. date: today --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} This vignette — the table selection, the PyTorch and `mirt` code, the analysis design, and the writing below — was produced largely by Claude (Anthropic), working from a task specification and with human review. Check `nn_irt_helpers.py`, `nn_irt_mirt_compute.R` and `nn_irt_estimation.py` directly if you are relying on the numbers here. ::: ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} **Exploratory.** I pick these questions after looking at the data; the tables are whatever IRW happens to hold, not a sample of anything; and nothing here corrects for the many comparisons a corpus-wide sweep involves. So treat what follows as suggestive. Some of it is also simply wrong: across this many tables there will be mislabelled columns, fits that did not converge, and coding errors that survived review. If a result matters to you, read the compute script and refit it yourself — and [tell me what you find](https://github.com/ben-domingue/irw/issues). ::: # Part I. The 2PL as a neural network {#part-i} ## Motivation A logistic item response model is a very small neural network. The Rasch model takes a person, looks up one number for them ($\theta_p$), takes an item, looks up one number for it ($d_i$, the negative of the difficulty), adds the two, and passes the sum through a sigmoid. In PyTorch terms that is two `nn.Embedding` layers and no hidden layer at all. The 2PL adds a second item lookup, the slope $a_i$, and multiplies before it adds. Once the models are written this way, a question that is awkward to pose in the psychometric idiom becomes the obvious next step: what happens when the network is made wider or deeper? Does a neural network predict item responses better than the 2PL? Both words are defined precisely below, but in short: width is how many numbers the network looks up for each person and item, and depth is how many layers sit between those numbers and the predicted response. The question is not new. Variational IRT [@wu2020variational] and the recommender-systems literature [@koren2009matrix; @he2017ncf] both treat person-by-item data as a matrix to be factorised and have explored exactly these widenings. What is missing is a comparison on an honest footing: the same held-out cells, the same prior on persons, the same scoring rule, across enough real tables of different kinds to see where a wider network helps and where it does not. That is the contribution here. We build the classical models in PyTorch, confirm that they recover what `mirt` [@chalmers2012mirt] recovers, widen and deepen them, and score every model on held-out responses from 24 IRW tables with the InterModel Vigorish [IMV, @domingue2024imv], which puts every gain on the scale of a bet. Two flexible one-dimensional models from `mirt`, the monotonic polynomial [@falk2016monotonic] and the logistic positive exponent [@samejima2000lpe], join the comparison, because they make the opposite move from the networks: they change the *shape* of the item curve while keeping a single dimension. The short version of the answer, for these 24 tables and these fits, is that on a test built to measure one thing no network beat the 2PL by much, and that where a network did gain, a two-dimensional MIRT usually gained about as much as the larger networks, with a couple of exceptions we name. These are observations about specific models on hand-picked tables, from a single split, not a verdict on neural networks. They hold at the sizes we fit here: tables are capped at 5,000 respondents and 116 items, and scale is the one advantage a wider network is supposed to have, so a null is a null at this scale. They also hold for these estimators: none of the networks puts a prior on the item slopes, and that matters for how often a two-dimensional model finds its second dimension, a point we return to in the [limitations](#limitations). The page is in three parts. [Part I](#part-i) builds the models and checks them against `mirt`. [Part II](#part-ii) widens and deepens them on the 24 tables. One of the comparisons also turned up a small but consistent gap between the same 2PL fit in torch and in `mirt`; [Part III](#part-iii) takes it apart. ## Data and methods ### Dataset selection We wanted tables that would spread across the kinds of structure a wider network might find, rather than a random sample of the warehouse. The 24 tables fall into five groups, fixed in `nn_irt_helpers.py`: - **Achievement and ability tests** built to measure one thing (a Brazilian medical residency exam, an ENCCEJA Portuguese form, a Dutch listening test, a general intelligence measure, two vocabulary and ability samples). - **Knowledge tests with heterogeneous content** (two COVID-19 knowledge scales, a financial literacy test, the Author Recognition Test), where the items range over topics and a single dimension is a convenience rather than a design. - **Tests with a documented multidimensional structure** (the ECPE grammar test with its three-attribute Q-matrix, a mental-rotation test, a medical licensing exam). - **Personality and clinical inventories** that mix several syndromes or facets in one table (the Woodworth Psychoneurotic Inventory, the NPI, the Taylor Manifest Anxiety scale, the Eysenck EPI, the MCMI, and four more). - **Developmental screeners** (the ASQ and Denver items from the D-score project), which span motor, language and social domains and are age-adaptive, so each child answers only a slice of the items. All are dichotomous, and all but the two screeners are close to fully crossed: nearly every person answered nearly every item. The response values are checked at fetch time rather than trusted from metadata; one candidate, `vocabulary_iq`, turned out to be polytomous despite its metadata and was dropped (and the metadata corrected upstream); two further candidates, `encceja_2025_em_cn` and `mgkt_options`, were dropped because their full exports fail to load, so the final 24 is a design choice filtered by what we could read. Tables with more than 5,000 respondents or 116 items are subsampled to those caps with a fixed seed, so that every fit on the page stays small enough to run on a laptop. This selection is deliberate and it is *not* a sample: these 24 tables were picked to span kinds of structure, which makes them good for showing where gains come from and bad for estimating how often gains occur. That second question needs a rule-based selection over the whole warehouse, and this page does not answer it. ::: {#cell-data .cell execution_count=2} ::: {#data .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `prepare` calls `irw.fetch`, caches the table, subsamples, assigns integer indices, and draws the holdout mask with a fixed seed. Sizes are after subsampling. ### Held-out cells, not held-out people Every model here has a parameter per person. A model cannot predict a person it has never seen, so the usual split by rows (train on some people, test on others) is not available without a separate scoring step. We hold out **cells** instead. Within each person, 20% of the responses, chosen at random, are **test** cells: hidden during training and used only to score the models. A further 10% are **validation** cells, used only to decide when to stop training. The remaining 70% train. Every person and every item stays in the training set, and the same three-way mask is used by every model, including the `mirt` fits, which see the validation and test cells as missing. This is the cross-validation design of the IMV paper, and it fixes what is being predicted: a response the table already contains, from a person and an item the model has seen, with the remaining responses of that person in hand. On the two age-adaptive screeners, that means predicting items a child was actually given, not items the screener skipped. Predicting the responses of new people would be a different target, and would need a different design. One step looks at held-out outcomes, and we report it rather than hide it: if an item is constant in the training cells, one held-out cell with the other response is moved into training so the item can be fit. The table above counts how often that happens. ### The models, written as networks The four model classes below are the whole of the modelling code. Each takes a batch of person indices and item indices and returns a logit. | Model | Person lookup | Item lookup | Combine | Parameters | On the residency exam | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Rasch | $\theta_p$ (1 number) | $d_i$ (1 number) | $\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + J$ | 3,339 | | 2PL | $\theta_p$ (1) | $a_i, d_i$ (2) | $a_i\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + 2J$ | 3,455 | | MIRT, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf a_i$ ($k$), $d_i$ | $\mathbf a_i \cdot \boldsymbol\theta_p + d_i$ | $kN + (k+1)J$ | 6,794 | | Multilayer perceptron (MLP), $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf v_i$ ($k$) | $\mathrm{MLP}([\boldsymbol\theta_p, \mathbf v_i])$ | $kN + kJ + $ decoder | 6,775 (small), 11,223 (large) | Here $N$ is the number of persons and $J$ the number of items, and the residency exam column counts parameters for the first table on the page (3,223 persons, 116 items, $k = 2$). The decoder of the small MLP has 97 weights and that of the large one 4,545, so even the large network is mostly embeddings: the step from one dimension to two more than doubles the parameter count, and the larger decoder adds comparatively little on top. Two words carry the argument from here on, so it is worth pinning them down. **Width** is the size of the embeddings: how many numbers the network looks up for each person and for each item, written $k$ in the table above. Widening a model is adding latent dimensions, so a wider 2PL is a multidimensional 2PL and nothing more exotic than that; the Rasch model and the 2PL have width 1, and every wider model on this page has width 2. **Depth** is the number of hidden layers between the embeddings and the logit. The Rasch model, the 2PL and the MIRT have none: the looked-up numbers are combined by a dot product and that sum *is* the logit. The two MLPs have one and two hidden layers respectively. Put differently, width governs what the model can represent about a person and an item, and depth governs how freely what has been represented is allowed to combine. A dot product says that a person's standing on each dimension pays off additively and at a rate set by the item; depth lets that payoff bend. The 2PL is the width-1, depth-0 corner of this space, and every other model here moves away from it in one direction or the other --- which is what makes "is a bigger network better?" a question with two separate answers rather than one. The models are written in slope-intercept form, $a_i\theta_p + d_i$, as `mirt` writes them, rather than the textbook $a_i(\theta_p - b_i)$. This is not cosmetic. In the textbook form the gradient for $b_i$ is scaled by $a_i$, so the difficulties of weak items barely move during training, and a slope kept positive by an exponential cannot fit an item keyed against the trait, which several of the inventories below contain. The slope here is signed and unconstrained. The MIRT model is the compensatory multidimensional 2PL [@reckase2009mirt]: $k$-dimensional person and item embeddings combined by a dot product, which is also a factorisation of the person-by-item logit matrix whose interaction part has rank at most $k$ (the item intercepts add one more). With $k=1$ it is the 2PL; we use $k=2$. The multilayer perceptron, the plain feed-forward neural network and the thing most people mean by "a neural net", concatenates the two embeddings and passes them through one or more hidden layers of rectified linear units before a final linear layer produces the logit. The interaction between person and item is then no longer constrained to be a dot product; this is the shape used in neural collaborative filtering [@he2017ncf]. We fit two sizes, both on $k=2$ embeddings: a small one with a single hidden layer of 16 units, and a large one with two hidden layers of 64. The step from one to the other adds a layer, widens the layers and multiplies the decoder's weights by about 50 all at once, so it is a step from a small decoder to a large one rather than a clean test of depth alone. ### Estimation The PyTorch models are fit by minibatch gradient descent (Adam) on the mean negative log-likelihood plus a penalty on the person parameters, the one a $N(0,1)$ prior on $\theta_p$ would contribute (the section that follows builds this up line by line). It is tempting to call the result a maximum a posteriori estimate, but with free item slopes that is not quite right: the penalty does not by itself pin down the scale of $\theta$, for a reason step 5 spells out, and what keeps each fit finite is early stopping. Each model is trained once for 30 epochs, with one optimiser, and the parameters from the epoch with the lowest validation loss are kept. So the networks on this page are early-stopped joint fits with a penalty on the persons. The alternative is to standardise $\theta$ to mean zero and SD one inside the model, which does fix the scale; [Part III](#part-iii) fits every model both ways and reports what that costs. The body of the page uses the penalised version. The `mirt` models are fit offline by marginal maximum likelihood [@bock1981marginal] on the same training cells, in `nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`, and each held-out cell is predicted by its posterior-predictive probability: the item curve integrated over the person's posterior on a quadrature grid. Three models are fit this way: the 2PL again, as the marginal-likelihood anchor for the PyTorch 2PL; the monotonic polynomial model, whose item curve is a flexible monotone function rather than a logistic; and the logistic positive exponent (LPE) model, whose item curve is asymmetric. ### Scoring Every model is scored on the same held-out cells by log-loss and by the IMV against the PyTorch 2PL. The IMV converts a log-loss improvement into a bet: if model 0 predicts held-out responses as well as a coin with bias $w_0$ and model 1 as well as a coin with bias $w_1$, the IMV is $(w_1 - w_0)/w_0$, the relative gain in the bettor's edge. The [IMV vignette](imv.qmd) has the derivation and the R package. In Python we use the [`imvpy`](https://github.com/intermodelvigorish/imvpy) package, whose `vanilla_imv` takes the baseline probabilities, the enhanced probabilities and the outcomes, in that order. The definition is short enough to write out, and the helper module does so; the two agree on the first table's held-out cells to the fourth decimal, the residual being how extreme probabilities are clipped. ::: {#imv-check .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` def imv(y: np.ndarray, p0: np.ndarray, p1: np.ndarray) -> float: """InterModel Vigorish of model 1 over model 0 on held-out cells.""" w0 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p0)) w1 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p1)) return (w1 - w0) / w0 helper imv 0.42432 imvpy 0.42432 ``` ::: ::: ## Building the network, step by step Before the comparison, we write the 2PL as a network from nothing but `torch`, on one table, so that each piece can be seen. The helper module used later is this code with bookkeeping added. ### 1. Long data is already the right shape A neural network consumes one training example at a time, and an item response is one example: a person index, an item index, a 0/1 outcome. Nothing has to be reshaped to a wide matrix; IRW's long format is the network's native input. Three integer-coded columns become three tensors. ::: {#f674730e .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (tensor([1946, 506, 1335, 1109, 3172]), tensor([0, 0, 0, 0, 0]), tensor([0., 0., 0., 0., 0.]), (3223, 116)) ``` ::: ::: ### 2. An embedding is a lookup table of parameters `nn.Embedding(n, k)` is an $n \times k$ table of trainable numbers. Indexing it with a tensor of integers returns the matching rows. A person embedding of width 1 is a column of $\theta_p$; an item embedding of width 1 is a column of $d_i$. There is no "input layer" in the usual sense: the index *is* the input. ::: {#f292ce9f .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (torch.Size([3223, 1]), tensor([[-0.2585], [ 1.3713], [ 0.3665]], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: ### 3. The forward pass is the item response function For the 2PL the logit is $a_i \theta_p + d_i$: look up three numbers and combine them. A `Module` packages the lookups and the combination, and its `forward` method is the item response function on the logit scale. The sigmoid that turns a logit into a probability is folded into the loss below, which is numerically safer than applying it here. ::: {#814cdf4c .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (tensor([ 0.1266, 0.0740, -0.1018, -0.0402, 0.0100], grad_fn=), tensor([0.5316, 0.5185, 0.4746, 0.4899, 0.5025], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: At initialisation every item has slope 1 and intercept 0 and every person is near 0, so every probability is about one half. ### 4. The loss is the negative log-likelihood `BCEWithLogitsLoss` is $-\frac{1}{n}\sum_c \big[y_c \log p_c + (1-y_c)\log(1-p_c)\big]$ with $p_c = \sigma(\text{logit}_c)$: the mean negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, which is exactly the quantity an IRT package maximises. Before training it is $\log 2 \approx 0.693$, the log-loss of a fair coin. ::: {#633034fb .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 0.6942976713180542 ``` ::: ::: ### 5. A prior on persons, but not on items Persons and items are both parameters here, but they are not in the same position. Each item is answered by hundreds or thousands of persons, so its slope and intercept are usually well determined by the data; the exception is an item that nearly everyone answers the same way, which [Part III](#part-iii) meets. Each person answers a dozen to a hundred items, and there is a new $\theta_p$ for every person added to the sample, so the person parameters never stop multiplying. Fitting a free $\theta_p$ for every person by maximum likelihood is joint maximum likelihood, which is inconsistent as the number of persons grows [@haberman1977maximum] and runs away for perfect scores. IRT software avoids this by integrating $\theta$ out under a $N(0,1)$ prior, which is marginal maximum likelihood [@bock1981marginal]; the item parameters are left as free fixed effects, exactly as they are here. The network's equivalent is to add $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_p \theta_p^2$ to the loss, scaled by $1/n$ to match the mean log-likelihood. That is a single line, and it stops any one person's $\theta_p$ running away. It does not do everything the prior does in `mirt`, though. The likelihood only ever sees the product $a_i\theta_p$, so dividing every $\theta_p$ by some $c > 1$ and multiplying every slope by $c$ leaves every predicted probability where it was and shrinks the penalty by $c^2$. With free slopes the penalised loss can therefore always be lowered a little further by shrinking the persons and growing the items, and it has no finite minimum of its own. What holds the fit in place is that training stops early, at the epoch where the loss on the validation cells is lowest, and the drift can be watched happening in [Part III](#part-iii) when the stopping is taken away. Nothing here puts a prior on the item slopes either. That keeps the networks comparable to one another, but it is not free for the multidimensional ones, and the [limitations](#limitations) say what it costs. The helper module's `fit` uses exactly this expression. ### 6. The training loop Gradient descent on the objective, in minibatches, with Adam as the optimiser. Each pass over the training cells is an epoch. This is the whole algorithm; everything else is monitoring. ::: {#6189df4f .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` epoch 1 train log-loss 0.5614 epoch 2 train log-loss 0.5424 epoch 3 train log-loss 0.5395 epoch 4 train log-loss 0.5386 epoch 5 train log-loss 0.5383 epoch 6 train log-loss 0.5381 epoch 7 train log-loss 0.5380 epoch 8 train log-loss 0.5379 epoch 9 train log-loss 0.5379 epoch 10 train log-loss 0.5378 ``` ::: ::: Ten epochs take a few seconds on a laptop CPU, and the training log-loss settles at the value the 2PL can reach on this table. Held-out predictions are the same forward pass on the held-out indices, through a sigmoid: ::: {#a585d1ce .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 0.5532593243534318 ``` ::: ::: That is a complete item response model, fit by a neural-network toolkit, in about thirty lines. The Rasch model drops the slope. The multidimensional model makes the embeddings wider. The MLP replaces the dot product with hidden layers. All four live in the helper module with the same training loop (`fit`), which also scores the validation cells after every epoch and keeps the parameters from the best one, the early stopping step 5 relies on, and records the train, validation and test loss as it goes. ## The network recovers what mirt recovers First, the Rasch and 2PL models from the helper module, trained with the same loop as above on the residency exam, each reported by its training and test log-loss at the epoch where its validation loss was lowest. The 2PL's held-out loss is the number to carry forward: everything else on the page is scored against it. ::: {#fit-one .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rasch best validation epoch 55 of 80: train log-loss 0.5478, test log-loss 0.5623 2PL best validation epoch 63 of 80: train log-loss 0.5377, test log-loss 0.5533 ``` ::: ::: Does the network recover the item parameters? The offline `mirt` 2PL fit wrote its slopes and intercepts next to its predictions, so we can compare item by item. ::: {#cell-fig-recovery .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-recovery-output-1.png){#fig-recovery width=978 height=428} ::: ::: The intercepts agree closely (a correlation of 0.995). The slopes agree once the scale of $\theta$ is accounted for: `mirt` fixes the *population* variance of $\theta$ at one, while the network's point estimates are shrunk by the penalty and have a smaller spread, so its raw slopes are proportionally larger. Multiplying them by the spread of $\hat\theta$ puts the two on roughly the same footing here, with a correlation of 0.992 and the rescaled slopes a median 4% above `mirt`'s. That is a check that the two fits tell the same story about these items, not a general way to recover population-scale slopes from a joint fit. The remaining scatter is the difference between a point estimate for each person and integrating the person out, to which we return below. # Part II. Width and depth on 24 tables {#part-ii} ## Wider networks overfit, and early stopping is the fix Now the models that are not classical IRT, still on the residency exam. Before looking, it helps to say what to expect. Training loss should roughly fall in order of parameter count: the Rasch model is a special case of the 2PL and the 2PL of the MIRT, so each of those can fit the cells it is shown at least as well as the one before it, and the MLPs, though not exact supersets of the MIRT, have more freedom still. So the Rasch curve should sit highest, the 2PL below it, and the three wider models below that. Held-out loss is a different matter. Extra parameters only help there if they capture something that generalises from a person's training cells to their held-out ones; if they do not, the model spends its freedom memorising the training cells, and validation loss turns upward after an early minimum. On a test built to measure one thing, the anticipation is therefore that the wider models will win on the left panel and lose on the right, and that the losing will be worst for the model with the most parameters. ::: {#cell-fig-curves .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-curves-output-1.png){#fig-curves width=979 height=429} ::: ::: That is what happens. On the left, the Rasch and 2PL curves flatten within ten epochs at the value each model can reach, and the three wider models keep going, ending about 0.01 below the 2PL in training loss. On the right, the 2PL's validation curve is nearly flat and it ends as the best model. The MIRT model comes within about 0.001 of it at its third epoch and then drifts upward, ending 0.005 behind; the small multilayer perceptron does the same; the large one is at its best at the fourth epoch and by epoch thirty has given back 0.008 of that, ending 0.009 behind the 2PL and behind even the Rasch model, having fit the training cells better than anything else on the page. The gap between the two panels is overfitting made visible, and it widens with parameter count, as anticipated. Two practical consequences follow. First, the wider models have to be stopped early, and their best validation epoch arrives fast, after three or four passes over the data, so every model in the comparison below is reported at its best validation epoch rather than at convergence. Second, the test length matters: a person with 81 training responses, as here, pins their $\theta_p$ down well enough that the 2PL barely overfits at all, which is why its validation curve is flat. On shorter tests even the 2PL starts to drift, and we return to that below. ### Held-out IMV across 24 tables ::: {#cell-fig-imv .cell execution_count=15} ::: {#fig-imv .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## On tests built to measure one thing, no network beat the 2PL by much Across the achievement and ability tests, the knowledge tests and two of the three exams with a documented multidimensional structure, the wider networks sit within about 0.01 IMV of the 2PL, and as often below it as above, with one or two exceptions noted below. For calibration, the IMV paper puts the gain from 1PL to 2PL on typical cognitive data at roughly the value of knowing someone's age when predicting chronic disease; the gains here are a fraction of that, and they go both ways. The ECPE grammar test is the instructive case. It has a known three-attribute Q-matrix, and a two-dimensional model still predicts no better. One reading is that the attributes are too correlated to carry separate signal in held-out cells, but nothing here tests that, and a two-dimensional fit to a three-attribute design that fails to find its second dimension (see the [limitations](#limitations)) would look the same. What can be said is narrower: structure that is real in the design need not show up in prediction. The one clear exception in this group is the FSIQ mental-rotation test, where every wider network gains about 0.03. Whatever it was built to measure, in held-out prediction it does not behave as a one-dimensional test. What the second dimension is, prediction alone cannot say, and we have not read the items. ## Where the networks win, a two-dimensional 2PL mostly wins too The two-dimensional MIRT gains more than 0.005 on seven of the 24 tables: about 0.03 on the ADQ anhedonia scale and the mental-rotation test, 0.02 on the Eysenck EPI (three scales in one table) and the Denver screener, 0.01 on the GMI, and smaller amounts on the Woodworth and the Author Recognition Test. On the other seventeen it is within 0.005 of the 2PL, so the positive result rests on a minority of these tables. On most of the seven, the MLPs match or trail the MIRT, and across all 24 the large MLP is no better than the small one on average (the two differ by $-0.0001$, with the table-by-table differences running from $-0.02$ to $+0.01$). There are two exceptions worth naming. On the Denver screener both MLPs gain about 0.04, twice what the MIRT gains, and on the 18-response Onah knowledge test the small MLP gains 0.011 where the MIRT loses 0.007. Neither is large enough, alone, to say that a nonlinear decoder finds something a second dimension misses, and with a single split we cannot tell either from noise. So the summary for these data is modest: most of what these two decoders found, a two-dimensional 2PL found as well, and we see no general advantage for the larger decoder. What a second dimension *is* on a given instrument is a question about the instrument, and held-out prediction cannot answer it. The Rasch row shows the same thing from the other side. Its large losses (0.11 on the NPI, 0.09 on the ADQ, 0.07 on the Denver screener) are tables where slopes differ sharply across items. In IRW the responses are as deposited, not recoded to a common direction, so some of those slopes are items keyed against the rest of the test, which a Rasch model cannot fit at all; the Rasch row is a baseline on the raw coding. The step from one item parameter to two is worth more than every step after it. ## Flexible item curves do not add much The asymmetric LPE curve tracks the `mirt` 2PL to within 0.002 on every table, very slightly above it on average (+0.0004). The monotonic polynomial is a little better on several tests (0.014 on the mental-rotation test), and worse on several inventories (0.044 below on the NPI, 0.015 on the ADQ, 0.009 on the Woodworth), and on five tables it had not converged after 1,000 EM cycles, so its row is the least trustworthy on the page. Changing the shape of the item curve while keeping one dimension buys a little on some tables and loses more on others. The [asymmetric IRT vignette](asymmetric_irt.qmd) reaches the same verdict from a different direction, taking the three asymmetric models of @shimbonifay2026 across dozens of binary IRW tables with the same IMV: the plain 2PL wins outright on the largest share, and the best case in that batch is worth about what a typical 1PL-to-2PL upgrade is worth. On dichotomous tables the 2PL's logistic curve is good enough, and the only thing worth adding is a dimension, when the instrument has one to add. ## The mirt 2PL gap goes with the estimator, and it is largest on short tests The same 2PL fit by marginal maximum likelihood beats the gradient-descent fit by 0.03 on the 25-item COVID knowledge test, by about 0.01 on the 30-item ENCCEJA form, the listening test and the 18-item financial literacy test, and by 0.001 on the 116-item residency exam. The largest gap, 0.05, is on the Denver screener, which has 105 items but is age-adaptive: each child answers only the items near their age, about two dozen in training, so it is a short test in the sense that matters. (On the Denver and the ASQ `mirt`'s 2PL had not converged after 1,000 EM cycles, so their exact values should not be leaned on.) Plotting the gap against the number of training responses each person contributes makes the pattern plain. ::: {#cell-fig-gap .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-gap-output-1.png){#fig-gap width=649 height=385} ::: ::: Why does it happen? The networks here treat each person's $\theta$ as a parameter to be estimated, and the item parameters are then fit around those point estimates. With a dozen or twenty responses per person those estimates are poor, and the item parameters inherit the error, which is the incidental-parameter problem; `mirt` integrates the persons out instead. That is a story about the estimator rather than the model, and it is worth more than a paragraph, so [Part III](#part-iii) takes it apart. We have left the network as it is so that the effect stays visible here: it is the price of the simplest possible estimator, and readers who build their own networks should know it is there. # Part III. Which estimator closes the gap to mirt? {#part-iii} [Part II](#part-ii) left a promise unkept: the same 2PL, fit in torch and in `mirt`, does not give the same held-out loss, and the gap is largest on short tests. This part takes it apart. It is an aside rather than part of the main argument, which is why it is short, but anyone who builds the networks above will meet the same gap --- and one of our attempts to close it was wrong in an instructive way. Two things differ between the torch 2PL and the `mirt` 2PL. One is how the scale of the person parameters is set: the PyTorch 2PL puts an $N(0,1)$ penalty on $\theta$, while `mirt` fixes its population variance by assumption. The other is the estimator: the PyTorch model is fit by gradient descent on the joint likelihood, with each person's $\theta$ treated as a parameter, while `mirt` integrates the persons out. We fit the same 2PL six ways on the same training cells, scored on the same held-out cells, to separate the two. The six are: **Adam with the prior**, the network used throughout the page; **Adam constrained**, with $\theta$ standardised in the forward pass and no penalty; **alternating JML**, Newton block updates of persons and items in turn, in both a prior and a constrained version; **EM marginal maximum likelihood**, the estimator `mirt` uses, with a posterior over a quadrature grid; and **MML by L-BFGS**, the same marginal likelihood maximised directly with autograd. The joint and alternating estimators predict with point estimates of $\theta$; EM and MML predict with the posterior. One thing to note before the table: as step 5 of [Part I](#part-i) showed, the penalty does not fix the scale at all. In the likelihood $a_i\theta_p$ is all that matters, so the same fit can be written with a smaller $\theta$ and a larger $a$ at a lower penalty, and the penalised objective keeps rewarding that trade. Run alternating JML without early stopping on the residency exam and over 2,000 sweeps the person SD falls from 0.55 to 0.04 while the median slope rises from 1.1 to 14 --- with the held-out log-loss at 0.5538 after 100 sweeps and 0.5539 after 2,000, because $a\theta$ is what the likelihood sees. The constrained version fixes the scale exactly, and that is the only difference between the two alternating fits. ::: {#cell-fig-estimators .cell execution_count=19} ::: {#fig-estimators .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The routines that fit by marginal likelihood and predict from the posterior sit above zero, by about +0.006 on average; the ones that fit persons and items jointly and plug in a point estimate of $\theta$ sit at or below zero on average. The two pipelines differ in two things at once, though: how the item parameters are estimated, and whether the person is integrated out when a held-out cell is predicted. This comparison does not separate those (the [limitations](#limitations) say more), so the honest summary is that the marginal-likelihood pipeline, taken whole, closes the gap. The +0.006 is also the `mirt 2PL` row of @fig-imv, which is where this question came from. **Alternation does not help.** Alternating joint maximum likelihood is the textbook way to fit a joint model, and here it is worse than Adam, by 0.002 for the prior version and by 0.012 for the constrained one. That is consistent with the incidental-parameter problem, though the alternating fits also carry bounds on $\theta$ and the slopes that Adam does not, so it is not a clean test of it. The best validation sweep falls within the first ten on 13 of 24 tables for the prior version (median eight) and on 23 of 24 for the constrained one (median two), and both stop on patience rather than convergence on most tables. On short tests the loss then rises, as some items separate the persons and their slopes run to the bound. The constrained fit is worst on the Onah test, 18 training responses per person, where it trails `mirt` by 0.15. ## Constraining the scale does not close it, and it costs a little Standardising $\theta$ to mean zero and SD one in the sample removes the drift above (it fixes the first two moments, not the shape, and with two dimensions it does not make them uncorrelated). On the residency exam it recovers `mirt`'s item parameters about as well as the prior version does: intercepts agree closely in both, and slopes agree once the scale is handled, the constrained ones a median 3% above `mirt`'s and the rescaled prior ones 4% above. Each panel scores one network's constrained fit against **the same network fit with the prior**, so a dot at zero means fixing the scale changed nothing for that model on that table, and a dot below zero means it cost something. Nothing is compared across panels, which is why the Rasch panel can sit at zero while the MLP panels sit below it without that being a statement about Rasch versus an MLP. The Rasch panel is worth pausing on, because in an earlier version of these fits it told us something false. With the Rasch model written the usual way --- $\theta_p + d_i$, no slope --- the constraint was catastrophic: worse on every one of the 24 tables, by 0.03 on average and by 0.19 on the Onah test. That is not what it costs to fix the scale. It is what it costs to fix the scale with nothing left to absorb it. The penalised version lets the data set the spread of $\theta$, which comes out at 0.56 on the residency exam and 0.17 on the Onah test, and a slopeless Rasch has no way to express that the spread should not be one. Giving it a single slope $c$ shared by every item --- still a Rasch model, since the items continue to differ only in difficulty --- removes most of the problem: the constrained Rasch is then $0.002$ behind the penalised version on average and ahead of it on 10 of the 24 tables. The lesson is about identification, not about the constraint: a model that cannot represent the scale should not be asked to fix it. With that repaired, the cost of the constraint is small and consistent across the five networks: the panel means run from $-0.002$ for the Rasch model to $-0.006$ for the large MLP. In four of the five panels it is also concentrated where theory says it should be. The Rasch model, the 2PL, the MIRT and the small MLP all fan out below zero at the left, where people answer few items, and close toward the zero line at the right; the correlations printed under the figure run from +0.37 to +0.61 for those four, and the spread of the costs halves or better between the short tables and the long ones. The large MLP is the exception and worth noting as one: it pays about $-0.006$ whatever the test length, and its correlation is the $-0.06$ at the end of that printed line. Whatever it is losing to the constraint is not the thing short tests cause. Standardising $\theta$ divides out the spread of estimates that are mostly noise on a short test, stretching poorly determined person parameters back to a spread of one instead of shrinking them toward zero. That is the incidental-parameter story again, seen from the other side. The constraint also does nothing to stop the wide networks overfitting: they reach their best validation loss early and climb after it in both versions. Early stopping is still what keeps them honest. # Limitations ## Of the model comparison - **One split, one seed, no uncertainty.** Every number on the page comes from a single draw of the train/validation/test cells and a single initialisation. We report no standard errors, and differences of a few thousandths of an IMV point could change sign under another draw. Where the text calls a difference small or describes models as tied, that is a description of these fits, not an equivalence test. Stopping uses the validation cells and never the test cells, so the reported numbers are not flattered by the choice of epoch. - **Two estimators, one model.** The PyTorch 2PL (a penalised, early-stopped joint fit by gradient descent) and the `mirt` 2PL (marginal maximum likelihood) are the same model and do not give the same held-out loss. The comparison that is fair is therefore networks against the PyTorch 2PL and flexible curves against the `mirt` 2PL, and Parts I and II are written that way. Part III shows that fitting by marginal likelihood and predicting from the posterior closes the gap in torch, and that fixing the scale of $\theta$ does not. - **Only person and item identities enter the model.** The networks see exactly what the classical models see, so this is a comparison of functional forms, not of information. Sequential models of learning [@piech2015dkt] use the order of responses; models with item text as input can predict items never seen in training. These use more than the (person, item, response) triple. Variational IRT, which replaces the per-person point estimates with an encoder network, need not: it can be built on exactly these data, and is the most natural next model for this page. All of them can be scored with the same held-out cells and the same IMV, but none is on this page. - **Dichotomous, dense tables only.** The cell-level split and the Bernoulli loss are written for 0/1 responses. Polytomous tables need a different output layer and a different loss; sparse tables raise the question of whether the missingness is informative. - **Subsampling.** Tables are capped at 5,000 respondents and 116 items. The gains reported for the inventories are therefore gains at that size; a wider network may do relatively better with more data, which is the usual pattern and is not tested here. - **Twenty-four tables, chosen by hand.** The groups were picked to span kinds of structure, not sampled from the warehouse, and the counts per group are small. The sizes of the gains are specific to these tables. Because the set was chosen to span kinds of structure, it is likely enriched for gains, and the share of tables that gain here (seven of 24) should not be read as a rate for the warehouse. - **No regularisation of the item side.** Every network here leaves its item parameters free (step 5 of Part I), and that matters most for the two-dimensional models, whose second dimension may fail to emerge and leave a fit that predicts like the 2PL. We have seen this outside the page: on 50 other IRW tables, `mirt`'s two-factor model fit without a slope prior predicted exactly as the 2PL did on 28, and with a lognormal prior on the slopes on one. That prior both shrinks the slopes and forces them positive, so the check does not say which of the two does the work, and it is not a test of the networks themselves. What it does say is that a two-dimensional fit that gains nothing is a fact about the fit before it is a fact about the table, and we read the MIRT k=2 results that way. The penalties also do different jobs in different models: the same person penalty on an MLP can be undone by larger weights in its first layer, so "no slope prior" does not put the MIRT and the MLPs under identical regularisation either. ## Of the estimator comparison - **Two estimators are on a common footing; the networks are not.** The MML fits are the same model as `mirt` and are compared directly. The Adam networks and the alternating JML fits are different estimators of the same model, and their gaps to `mirt` are gaps in estimation, not in the model. - **Stopping uses the validation cells.** The Adam networks and both alternating JML fits pick their stopping point on the validation cells; the MML fits do not use them at all, and maximise the training likelihood (EM, then four L-BFGS rounds). None of the estimators sees the test cells. - **Bounds on the alternating fits.** Alternating JML bounds each $\theta_p$ at $\pm 6$ and each slope at $\pm 6$, because unpenalised JML has no finite optimum on an item the persons separate. Adam and the MML fits have no such bounds. Part of the alternating fits' ranking may reflect the bounds rather than the estimator, and we have not checked how much. - **Estimation and prediction change together.** The joint fits predict by plugging in a point estimate of $\theta_p$; the MML fits integrate over each person's posterior. Part III compares the two pipelines as wholes. It does not separate how much of the MML advantage comes from the item parameters and how much from integrating at prediction time. - **Items with extreme parameters.** On the ASQ, Denver and EDSC screeners several items have parameters in the hundreds, and the marginal likelihood is flat along them. Two correct maximisers can stop at different points there, which is why the largest MML disagreements with `mirt` are on those tables. - **Dichotomous 2PL only.** The estimators here are for the 2PL on 0/1 responses, and the multidimensional and nonlinear networks are not refit with them. # Reproducibility **Source code for this page:** [`nn_irt.qmd`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt.qmd), [`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py), [`nn_irt_chart.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_chart.py), [`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R), and, for Part III, [`nn_irt_estimation.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation.py), [`nn_irt_estimation_compute.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_compute.py) and [`nn_irt_estimation_drift.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_drift.py).
